lesson_title: The Bat's Four-Millimetre Trick: Hunting With Sound
hook_text: A bat catches a moth in pitch darkness — using waves exactly the size of the moth. That is not luck.
clip_script: Why does a bat squeak at a pitch no human will ever hear? Not for drama — it is shopping for small things. Here is the rule of the shop: a wave only bounces properly off things about its own size or bigger. Watch a harbour: long rolling swells slide past a mooring pole as if it were not there, but tiny ripples scatter off the same pole. Now price the bat's purchase. Calling at eighty-five thousand vibrations per second buys waves four millimetres long — moth-sized waves. To a four-millimetre wave, a moth is a billboard: the squeak slaps off it and sprints home. If the bat called at our speaking pitch, its metre-long waves would pour around the moth like the swell around the pole. The moth would not exist. Then the timing: the squeak returns after fifteen thousandths of a second, so the round trip was five point one metres — halve it, and there is a moth two and a half metres ahead. Ships run the same trick and call it sonar. Hospitals run it and call it ultrasound, watching a baby with echoes because sound is gentle and X-rays are not. One physics: squeak short, time the echo, halve the trip.
visual_style: Night sky scene with a bat emitting glowing pulse rings that shrink to millimetre scale; a moth lighting up as the pulse strikes and reflects; split-screen morph to a ship pinging the seabed and a scanner tracing a baby; numbers count the echo timing.
mood: A nature-documentary hunt that turns out to be a physics masterclass.
pacing: Slow mysterious open in the dark, sharp acceleration at the squeak-and-echo, satisfying halving reveal, quick triple-application ending.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and make every echo and sonar question routine.
